sections.heading: Asphalt Shingle Roofing We Provide in Newark, NJ

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing installs 2 asphalt shingle systems across Essex County: 3-tab shingles and architectural shingles — for residential and commercial sloped roofs.

runs.v: Asphalt shingle roofing layers fiberglass-mat shingles, synthetic underlayment, an eave-and-valley ice barrier, metal drip edge, and flashing into a water-shedding system, the most common residential roof covering on roughly 73% of US homes, per 2024 roofing-market data.

A Newark Quality Roofing asphalt shingle install matches the shingle line and the attic ventilation to the Essex County climate, because 3-tab shingles last 20 years and architectural shingles 30 years, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart, and the NRCA notes actual asphalt life varies up to 40% with climate, install, and maintenance. Architectural shingles bond multiple layers of asphalt-saturated fiberglass mat into a dimensional profile that carries a higher wind rating than the single-layer 3-tab profile, per ARMA and manufacturer guidance. Homeowners generally choose among three primary styles of asphalt shingles: 3-tab, the budget option; architectural, the most popular roofing option in Newark; and luxury shingles, premium materials engineered to mimic natural materials like slate or wood shakes. Modern asphalt shingles come in many colors and profiles to complement various architectural styles and enhance curb appeal and aesthetic appeal, and light colors and cool-roof shingles provide an energy-efficient option by reflecting solar heat, though the shingles add little insulation. Most fiberglass asphalt shingles carry a Class A fire rating under ASTM E108 and UL 790, a step above Class B fire resistance.

c.v: Architectural shingle installation

items.v: — Architectural shingle installation fits laminated dimensional shingles that last 30 years and carry a wind rating up to 130 mph with the manufacturer 6-nail pattern, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart and ARMA and manufacturer guidance.

c.v: 3-tab shingle installation

items.v: — 3-tab shingle installation fits single-layer shingles that last 20 years and carry a wind rating near 60 mph, the lower-cost asphalt option, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart and ARMA guidance.

c.v: Ice barrier and synthetic underlayment

items.v: — Ice barrier and synthetic underlayment seal the deck at the eaves and valleys, where the IRC ice-barrier provision (R905.1.2) requires a self-adhering ice barrier from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line, per the International Residential Code.

c.v: Flashing and drip edge

items.v: — Flashing and drip edge seal the chimneys, walls, skylights, and valleys, the transitions the roofing industry estimates account for roughly 90–95% of roof leaks, an industry estimate attributed to the NRCA, with the drip edge extending at least 2 inches onto the deck, per GAF and ARMA.

c.v: Attic ventilation

items.v: — Attic ventilation balances soffit intake and ridge exhaust at 1 square foot of net-free vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor, because balanced ventilation extends roof service life by up to 25%, per the NRCA and ARMA.

sections.heading: Signs You Need Asphalt Shingle Roofing

c.v: An asphalt roof at or past its material lifespan

items.v: signals a new asphalt shingle roof, because 3-tab shingles last 20 years and architectural shingles 30 years, and actual asphalt life varies up to 40% with climate and maintenance, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart and the NRCA.

c.v: Granule loss with sandy grit in gutters and bald asphalt mat

items.v: indicates shingles nearing end of life; granule loss exceeding 30% of the surface is the common rule-of-thumb for beyond repair, and 50% loss cuts remaining life by up to 70%, per GAF.

c.v: Curling, cupping, and buckling shingles

items.v: indicate aging, trapped moisture, or undersized attic ventilation, the condition that accelerates shingle deterioration from the underside, per GAF and InterNACHI inspection guidance.

c.v: Cracked, torn, or wind-stripped shingles after a storm

items.v: expose the underlayment and the roof deck, because 3-tab shingles rate near 60 mph and NOAA classifies a thunderstorm as severe at wind gusts of 58 mph or higher, per ARMA and NOAA. Broken or missing shingles lead to water intrusion and can indicate the need for a roof replacement.

c.v: Damage across more than 25–30% of the roof area

items.v: crosses the contractor-consensus 25% rule, the threshold above which a full asphalt re-roof costs less than continued spot repair, per roofing industry guidance.

c.v: Brown or yellow ceiling stains that spread after rainfall

items.v: indicate an active roof leak or trapped attic moisture, the sign that points toward a failed flashing or shingle detail, per GAF and This Old House inspection guidance. Water stains on ceilings indicate a potential roof leak and, on an aging roof, a potential roof replacement.

sections.heading: What Is the 25% Rule for Roofing?

c.v: The 25% rule for roofing says that once damage covers more than about 25% of the roof area, a full roof replacement usually makes more sense than another repair.

runs.v: In New Jersey, N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 also requires a permit to repair over 25% of the roof in 12 months on any building but a detached one- or two-family home. Below that line, asphalt shingles can be replaced individually without needing to replace the entire roof, color-matched to the rest of the roof. Storm damage can lead to leaks and structural issues and needs fast roof repairs to prevent leaks: emergency roofing services respond quickly to storm damage, rapid emergency response is crucial for Newark residents, and a prompt emergency repair extends the life of the roof where patch solutions fail. To size the damage, contact Newark Quality Roofing by phone to schedule a free roof inspection.

sections.heading: How Our Roofing Contractors Perform Asphalt Shingle Roofing

runs.v: Deck, Ice Barrier, and Underlayment

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing contractors strip the roof to the deck, repair the sheathing, and install an ice barrier and synthetic underlayment before the shingles, the sequence that keeps the manufacturer system warranty intact.

runs.v: The IRC ice-barrier provision (R905.1.2) requires a self-adhering ice barrier from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line in ice-prone climates, and GAF directs a 36-inch self-adhered underlayment in valleys, per the International Residential Code and GAF installation guidance. Synthetic underlayment covers the remaining deck as a secondary water barrier, and metal drip edge extends at least 2 inches onto the deck at eaves and rakes, per GAF and ARMA.
Manufacturer-Specification Nailing

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing fastens each shingle in the manufacturer nailing zone with the correct nail count, because high-nailing above the sealant line leaves the lower edge unsecured and ranks among the most common uplift and leak causes.

runs.v: ARMA specifies nails penetrate at least three-quarters of an inch into solid deck, and the IBHS identifies improper installation and shingles unrated for the design wind speed as the 2 most common high-wind shingle-damage causes, per ARMA and the IBHS. Architectural shingles reach a wind rating up to 130 mph only with the manufacturer 6-nail pattern, per ARMA and manufacturer guidance, so a Newark Quality Roofing crew installs to the rated specification.
Flashing Integration and Balanced Ventilation

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing balances attic ventilation and integrates the flashing during the shingle coursing, sealing the transitions where most leaks originate.

runs.v: Step flashing weaves with each shingle course at walls, and the roofing industry estimates that roughly 90–95% of roof leaks originate at flashing and only 5–10% at the open shingle field, an industry estimate attributed to the NRCA. The NRCA and ARMA specify 1 square foot of net-free vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor, balanced about 50% intake and 50% exhaust, because balanced ventilation extends roof service life by up to 25%, per the NRCA.

sections.heading: Commercial Asphalt Shingle Roofing We Provide

On a commercial building, an asphalt shingle re-roof requires a permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, because the ordinary-maintenance exemption covers only the repair of up to 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code. sections.heading: How Long Do Asphalt Shingles Last in Newark's Climate?

c.v: Asphalt shingles typically last around 30 years in Newark, and aging roofs may need replacement after 20–30 years.

runs.v: 3-tab shingles have a shorter lifespan, typically 20–25 years, while architectural shingles are often rated for 30 years to a lifetime by their manufacturers, a warranty rating, not a service-life promise. New Jersey experiences hot summers and freezing winters that affect roofing choice: Newark roofs deal with baking sun, freeze-thaw cycles, and nor'easters with strong winds, and architectural shingles are designed to handle wind, rain, snow, and temperature swings, giving superior protection and durability. Among other roofing systems, metal roofs can last up to 50 years with proper care but cost more. Asphalt shingles require low maintenance and are easy to clean with a low-pressure rinse, never a pressure washer, and aging roofs show bald spots and granule loss first. Gutters need regular maintenance to prevent clogs; they protect homes from water intrusion and foundation damage, gutter systems should channel water away from foundations, and proper gutter installation can prevent basement flooding.

sections.heading: How to Tell If a Roofer Is Lying, and How to Choose One

c.v: The best roof repair contractors in Newark, NJ are registered, insured, local, and put everything in writing.

runs.v: New Jersey requires roofing contractors and siding contractors alike to register with the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the Contractors' Registration Act requires a written contract for any home improvement over $500, with three business days to cancel. Ask friends and neighbors in the community who they hired, and compare a free, no obligation estimate from more than one company: transparent pricing names the shingle line, underlayment, tear-off, and deck repair before the roof installation starts. A knowledgeable, professional roofer explains the job before installing anything, a responsive one returns calls in a timely manner, and customer care continues after the install. A roofer may be lying when claimed damage comes with no pictures, when high-pressure pricing demands a signature or cash deposit today, or when the contract has no registration number. A good experience looks like an excellent job: straight courses, sealed flashing, a clean yard, and a homeowner satisfied before the team collects final payment.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 3-tab and architectural shingles?

runs.v: Architectural shingles laminate several fiberglass-mat layers into a dimensional profile that lasts 30 years and rates up to 130 mph; 3-tab shingles are one flat layer that lasts 20 years and rates near 60 mph, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart and ARMA and manufacturer guidance.

faqs.q: How long do asphalt shingles last in the New Jersey climate?

runs.v: Architectural shingles last about 30 years and 3-tab shingles 20 years, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart, and actual life varies up to 40% with climate, installation, and attic ventilation, per the NRCA.

faqs.q: Should you repair or replace an asphalt shingle roof?

runs.v: Replace when damage exceeds 25–30% of the roof area or one repair approaches 50% of the replacement cost. Repair when the damage is localized on a roof under 10–15 years old, since individual shingles cost a fraction of a new roof.

faqs.q: Can asphalt shingles withstand the nor'easters and storms in Essex County?

runs.v: Yes, when rated and installed for it. Architectural shingles rate up to 130 mph with the manufacturer 6-nail pattern, well above the 58 mph gust threshold NOAA sets for a severe thunderstorm, per ARMA and manufacturer guidance.

faqs.q: Do you need a permit for asphalt shingle roofing in Newark, NJ?

runs.v: A complete re-roof of a detached one- or two-family home is ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and needs no construction permit. A commercial re-roof or a structural change to rafters or trusses does need a permit.

faqs.q: How much does asphalt shingle roofing cost in Essex County, NJ?

runs.v: Asphalt shingle roofing in New Jersey runs $5.50–$9.50 per square foot installed for 3-tab and $6.50–$11.00 for architectural shingles, against $3.50–$11.00 nationally. Newark Quality Roofing provides a free estimate in writing.

faqs.q: Can asphalt shingles be installed in winter in New Jersey?

runs.v: Yes, with cold-weather precautions: sealant strips need heat to bond, and Newark's average January low sits in the mid-20s °F, per NOAA normals at Newark Liberty, so winter installs hand-seal each shingle.
